Abstract Under equivalent stiffness conditions, material substitution based on a thin-walled
design is crucial for the lightweight of components. Developing high-performance steels with both
high-yield strength and excellent ductility has become a key focus in fields like aerospace and low
altitude flight. The novel low-density steel presented here exhibits a yield strength of 1 000 MPa,
which is 2–3 times higher than conventional low-alloy high-strength steels, while maintaining an
elongation of about 18.7%. By combining ex-situ experimental characterization with a phase
mechanical response model based on the iso-work theory and the von Mises equivalent method,
the role of heterogeneous deformation-induced strengthening was revealed. The calculated values
align closely with experimental results. This exceptional performance is attributed to a multiphase
heterogeneous microstructure, where fresh martensite, bainite/tempered martensite, and
deformation-induced martensite act as hard regions. These regions release micro-stresses through
inhomogeneous cooperative deformation with soft ferrite, enabling multiple plastic deformation
mechanisms and stress concentration relief. This research offers new insights into optimizing
microstructures through mechanical metallurgy, which is crucial for producing high-performance,
lightweight components.

1. Introduction
Energy conservation and emission reduction are essential
responsibilities for modern industry and crucial pathways
toward global sustainable development. Lightweight, one of
the most effective strategies for achieving these goals, is partic
ularly relevant in aerospace and low-altitude flight sectors,
where the use of advanced high-strength steels has become a
key trend. Studies show that reducing the total weight of air-
frames by 10% can enhance energy efficiency by 6%–8%.<sup>1,2</sup>
In this context, researchers are focused on developing third-
generation advanced high-strength steels, such as medium-
manganese steels and Quenching & Partitioning (Q&P) steels,
due to their exceptional strength-ductility balance.<sup>3,4</sup> These
materials have gained significant industrial attention for their
potential to meet lightweight demands. The microstructure
of Q&P steels typically consists of a martensitic matrix with
a controlled amount of metastable austenite. The martensite
provides high strength, while the metastable austenite
enhances work-hardening capacity through the
Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect during defor-
mation. However, increasing the carbon content to improve
strength compromises weldability, and raising the manganese
content narrows the Q&P process window, making it harder
to maintain product stability. These trade-offs complicate
efforts to improve the comprehensive mechanical properties
of Q&P steels. Medium-manganese steels (4wt%–12wt%
Mn) feature a dual-phase microstructure of ferrite and meta-
stable austenite, with a Product of Strength and Elongation
(PSE) reaching up to 30–40 GPa %.<sup>5,6</sup> However, the softer fer-
ritic matrix leads to lower yield strength, and the high man-
ganese content causes microsegregation in cast ingots.
Additionally, martensite formation during hot rolling compli-
cates the production of cold-rolled products, posing further
challenges for industrial-scale manufacturing. A pressing chal-
lenge lies in developing a structural material substitution
method that maintains strength and ductility while fulfilling
the demands of lightweight applications.

Micro-defects that develop in structural materials during
service can cause significant local stress concentrations, leading
to catastrophic failures and substantial losses of life and prop-
erty.<sup>7–10</sup> Studies show that reducing weight by 100 kg in struc-
tures like aircraft fuselage skins, engine casings, carrier frames,
and crash beams increases safety risks by 4%–6%.<sup>11</sup> There-
fore, it is imperative to develop new microstructural designs
that effectively mitigate these harmful effects while meeting
safety requirements and achieving lightweight construction.
Under external stress, crystal defects and interfaces can form
micropores, which subsequently expand and link into microc-
racks.<sup>12–14</sup> The significant stress concentration at crack tips
makes grain boundaries prone to tearing, gradually leading
to macroscopic fractures.<sup>15,16</sup> To address this issue, Xin et al.<sup>17</sup>
proposed introducing an appropriate number of grain bound-
aries to alleviate stress concentration-induced damage. While
this method contributes to balancing material strength and
ductility, it is not markedly effective in suppressing stress con-
centration and crack propagation. This indicates a need to
shift from a single-plane strain fracture mode to a multiple-
plane stress fracture mode, where the formation of multiple
microcracks can absorb substantial fracture energy. For
instance, Huang et al.<sup>18</sup> introduced high-density dislocations
into martensite and combined them with weaker grain bound-
ary interfaces to slow crack propagation, significantly enhanc-
ing the fracture toughness of the material. However, this
strategy imposes excessively high demands on the dislocation
storage capacity of material and is suitable primarily for situ-
ations involving sudden stress changes. Considering the load
conditions, to address the issues of material substitution and
lightweight in structural components during long-term service,
it is especially important to start with the design of extensive
dislocation interactions and accumulation.
Layered heterogeneous structures across multiple scales are
widely recognized for effectively regulating dislocation behav-
ior, which enhances plasticity and strengthens materials by
impeding dislocation movement.<sup>19–23</sup>
This coupling effect is
primarily due to Heterogeneous Deformation-Induced (HDI)
strengthening, driven by interactions between adjacent strain
fields during deformation.<sup>24</sup> Accumulating Geometrically Nec-
essary Dislocations (GNDs) at interfaces distributes local plas-
tic strain more uniformly, reducing stress concentrations and
improving strength and toughness.<sup>25–29</sup>
However, forming
multiscale heterogeneous structures remains challenging in
large-scale production. Leveraging key insights and following
the principle of ‘material simplification’, we developed novel
low-density steel that eliminates costly elements like Nb, Mo,
and Ni, while slightly increasing Al and Mn content. By using
mechanical-metallurgical methods that are easily applicable to
actual production, a multi-level microstructure is introduced
into this steel. The various mechanical responses promote the
coupling of multiple strengthening mechanisms, forming strain
gradients that effectively transmit stress and alleviate stress
concentration. This material significantly outperforms conven-
tional high-strength low-alloy steel by enhancing strength
while maintaining good ductility, opening new avenues for
lightweight structural design and innovative manufacturing
of high-performance large components.

blocking, bypassing, or cutting mechanisms. These interactions
make it difficult to describe material strength accurately using
linear superposition theory.<sup>51</sup> The effectiveness of various
strengthening mechanisms varies with the heterogeneous
deformation of microstructure, requiring a quantitative analy-
sis of phase composition and dislocation density.<sup>33,52</sup> The iso-
work theory provides a realistic and direct method for analyz-
ing the behavior of each phase during deformation.<sup>32</sup> It
assumes that tensile work is uniformly distributed across all
phases,<sup>34</sup> meaning that the product of the flow stress for each
phase and the corresponding true strain increment is equal:

Microscale strain localization can lead to the initiation of
microcracks, while the plastic anisotropy of different

voids (yellow dashed boxes) are mainly distributed at the inter-
face of the soft domain and hard domain. If the deformation is
severe enough, these voids will coalesce, leading to microvoid
coalescence fracture, as depicted in Fig. 11(a). In AN750-T
and AN800-T, the crack tip blunts at the hard domain inter-
face, generating secondary cracks (yellow arrows). The driving
force for crack propagation is lower than the resistance pro-
vided by the hard domains, allowing cracks to extend into
other easily nucleated areas. In AN850-T, the hard domains
were observed to be severed (red arrows). At 850 °??C, signifi-
cant migration of carbon and manganese into the B/TM and
FM regions results in local oversaturation of alloying ele-
ments, increasing the strength but also the brittleness of the
hard domains. The fracture morphology shows large dimples
surrounded by smaller ones (Fig. 11(b)). AN750-T displays rel-

some quasi-cleavage fractures, mostly originating from fresh
martensite. Dimple size distribution was analyzed using Nano
Measure software (Fig. 11(c)), revealing a bimodal distribu-
tion, with AN750-T having larger average dimple sizes. This
suggests that the coarse ferrite and fine hard phases effectively
alleviate stress concentration during deformation.

Appendix A.
A1. Selection of experimental materials and heat treatment
temperature
Weight reduction, a key strategy for energy conservation
and emissions reduction, has promoted the widespread use
of advanced high-strength steels in critical aerospace and low
altitude flight components. Third-generation steels, such as
medium-manganese and Q&P steels, typically require complex
processes like quenching, tempering, or microalloying, which,
despite their effectiveness, raise production costs.
This study introduces a novel low-density steel that elimi-
nates costly elements like Nb, Mo, and Ni, with a slight increase
in Mn and Al content. Higher Mn content lowers the critical
austenite temperatures (Ac1 and Ac3), stabilizing austenite at
lower temperatures during cooling and enabling retained austen-
ite at room temperature. It also slows the transformation to
pearlite, allowing bainite or martensite to form even at slower
cooling rates. Increasing the Al content can stabilize ferrite,
enhance its fraction during the cooling process, and reduce the
occurrence of incomplete bainite transformation, significantly
accelerating the kinetics of bainite formation. Moreover, the
addition of Al effectively lowers the density of the steel.
The specific measurement steps for the quenching phase
transformation experiment are shown in Fig. A1(a), and
Fig. A1(b) illustrates the trend of sample expansion with temper-
ature variation, where <sup>D</sup>L is the length variation of the measured
sample relative to its initial reference length during heat treat
ment (heating or cooling). Using the tangent method, the Ac1,
Ac3, Bf, and Ms temperatures of the experimental steel were
determined to be 705, 950, 380, 346 °??C, respectively, where Bf
represents the bainite transformation finish temperature and
Ms denotes the martensite transformation start temperature.
A critical zone annealing process was applied to adjust the pro
portion of ferrite and austenite, promoting the formation of a
multiphase structure during cooling to achieve a multi-level
microstructural strengthening effect. Aging in the lower bainite
region
( 4 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )
facilitates the refinement of bainitic structures,
controls the kinetics of bainite transformation, prevents pearlite
formation, and ensures excellent mechanical properties.
